message.content: {"schema_version":"teaching-unit.v0.4.0","input_manifest_sha256":"a8836a286f03bd004e024cabb37efa6b0a688d92bf9a450d69bb0e0d62300a29","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-tx-class-c:lineage:64","source_registry_sha256":"73669019241a96617275447ad5e45b56c17a2d4bd395699448d85850cfc5bafb","units":[{"unit_id":"sec02-u01","module_id":"sec02-m01","objective_ids":["sec02-u01"],"title":{"text":"Yearly inspection and sticker","fact_ids":["sec02-F01","sec02-F02","sec02-R01"]},"why_how":[{"text":"A yearly inspection catches unsafe equipment before it causes a crash, so every registered vehicle is checked.","fact_ids":["sec02-F01"]},{"text":"One sticker for both registration and inspection makes it easy for officers to confirm a vehicle is legal.","fact_ids":["sec02-F02"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Maria's car passes inspection in March, but she does not renew her registration until August.","fact_ids":["sec02-F02","sec02-R01"]},"reasoning":{"text":"A passing report counts toward registration for only ninety days from the inspection month.","fact_ids":["sec02-R01"]},"result":{"text":"By August her March report no longer counts, so she needs a fresh inspection before registering.","fact_ids":["sec02-R01","sec02-F02"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a passing inspection report counts toward registration for a whole year.","fact_ids":["sec02-R01"]},"correction":{"text":"Inspections repeat yearly, but each passing report counts only ninety days from its inspection month for registration.","fact_ids":["sec02-R01","sec02-F01"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Inspect yearly, register within ninety.","fact_ids":["sec02-F01","sec02-R01"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A neighbor passed inspection two months ago and plans to register now. Does the report still count?","fact_ids":["sec02-R01","sec02-F02"]},"answer":{"text":"Yes, because it is still within ninety days of the inspection month.","fact_ids":["sec02-R01"]},"rationale":{"text":"A passing report counts ninety days from its inspection month toward registration, so two months is inside that window.","fact_ids":["sec02-R01","sec02-F02"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec02-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Keeping your vehicle legal","fact_ids":["sec02-F01","sec02-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Every registered vehicle is inspected.","fact_ids":["sec02-F01","sec02-F02"]},{"text":"One sticker shows you are legal.","fact_ids":["sec02-F01","sec02-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson begins the section on vehicle inspection and registration. Driving safely depends on the driver, but it also depends on the vehicle. Texas requires every registered motor vehicle to pass a yearly safety inspection, and it uses a single sticker on the windshield to show that the vehicle is both registered and inspected. We will look at which vehicles need the inspection, what you must bring, how the inspection report is recorded, and how long a passing report stays useful when you go to register. Watch the timing rules, because they are easy to mix up.","fact_ids":["sec02-F01","sec02-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec02-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Who needs the yearly check","fact_ids":["sec02-F01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Every registered motor vehicle.","fact_ids":["sec02-F01"]},{"text":"Motorcycles, mopeds, scooters, autocycles too.","fact_ids":["sec02-F01"]},{"text":"Bring insurance proof for that vehicle.","fact_ids":["sec02-F01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Every motor vehicle registered in Texas must pass an inspection once a year at an official inspection station. That includes the vehicles people sometimes assume are exempt, such as motorcycles, mopeds, scooters, and autocycles. When you go to the station, you show proof of insurance for the vehicle being inspected. So the rule has no size exception. If a vehicle is registered in Texas and is a motor vehicle, it is inspected every year, and the insurance proof must match that vehicle. A small moped follows the same yearly rule as a family car or a pickup truck.","fact_ids":["sec02-F01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec02-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"One sticker, one database","fact_ids":["sec02-F02","sec02-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"The sticker proves registration and inspection.","fact_ids":["sec02-F02","sec02-R01"]},{"text":"Stations record passing reports electronically.","fact_ids":["sec02-F02","sec02-R01"]},{"text":"Reports count ninety days for registration.","fact_ids":["sec02-F02","sec02-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Texas now uses one valid windshield sticker to prove both registration and inspection together. When your vehicle passes, the station records a passing Vehicle Inspection Report in an electronic database. When you register, the motor vehicle department checks that database to confirm the inspection. For registration purposes, a passing report stays valid for ninety days from the inspection month. So the best habit is to register soon after you pass, while that report still counts. There is no separate inspection sticker anymore; the single registration sticker carries both meanings on the windshield.","fact_ids":["sec02-F02","sec02-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec02-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Timing the two steps","fact_ids":["sec02-F01","sec02-F02","sec02-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Inspect first, then register.","fact_ids":["sec02-F01","sec02-F02","sec02-R01"]},{"text":"Register while the report still counts.","fact_ids":["sec02-F01","sec02-F02","sec02-R01"]},{"text":"Carry insurance proof to both.","fact_ids":["sec02-F01","sec02-F02","sec02-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Putting the two steps in order helps. First, take the vehicle to an inspection station with proof of insurance and get a passing report. Second, register the vehicle while that report still counts, within ninety days of the inspection month. Once registration is done, the single windshield sticker shows both. Next year, the cycle starts again with a new inspection. If you wait too long between the two steps, the passing report expires for registration purposes, and you will need to have the vehicle inspected again before you can register it. Planning the two visits close together saves you a trip.","fact_ids":["sec02-F01","sec02-F02","sec02-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec02-u01-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Yearly versus ninety days","fact_ids":["sec02-R01","sec02-F01","sec02-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Inspection repeats every year.","fact_ids":["sec02-R01","sec02-F01","sec02-F02"]},{"text":"A report counts ninety days for registration.","fact_ids":["sec02-R01","sec02-F01","sec02-F02"]},{"text":"Two clocks, two purposes.","fact_ids":["sec02-R01","sec02-F01","sec02-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap built from two clocks. One clock is yearly: every registered vehicle must be inspected once a year. The other clock is ninety days: a passing report only counts toward registration for ninety days from the inspection month. Learners sometimes think a passing report covers registration for a full year because inspections are yearly. It does not. If a question asks how often a vehicle is inspected, think yearly. If it asks how long a passing report counts when you register, think ninety days. Keep the purpose of each clock in mind.","fact_ids":["sec02-R01","sec02-F01","sec02-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec02-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the report window","fact_ids":["sec02-R01","sec02-F02","sec02-F01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Passed two months ago.","fact_ids":["sec02-R01","sec02-F02","sec02-F01"]},{"text":"Does it still count?","fact_ids":["sec02-R01","sec02-F02","sec02-F01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: a neighbor's car passed inspection two months ago, and she plans to register it this week. Does that passing report still count toward registration? Work out your answer before reading on. Yes, it does, because it is still inside the ninety-day window from the inspection month. If she waited until five months had passed, the report would no longer count, and she would need a new inspection first. Either way, her car must also be inspected again next year, because the yearly inspection cycle is separate from the ninety-day registration window.","fact_ids":["sec02-R01","sec02-F02","sec02-F01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec02-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Inspection and sticker basics","fact_ids":["sec02-F01","sec02-F02","sec02-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Every registered vehicle, every year.","fact_ids":["sec02-F01","sec02-F02","sec02-R01"]},{"text":"One sticker proves both.","fact_ids":["sec02-F01","sec02-F02","sec02-R01"]},{"text":"Reports count ninety days.","fact_ids":["sec02-F01","sec02-F02","sec02-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us sum up. Every motor vehicle registered in Texas, including motorcycles, mopeds, scooters, and autocycles, must pass a yearly inspection at an official station, with insurance proof for that vehicle. A single windshield sticker now proves both registration and inspection. The station records the passing report electronically, and the motor vehicle department checks it when you register. That report counts toward registration for ninety days from the inspection month, while the inspection itself repeats every year. Next, we look at the brakes, lights, and other equipment a vehicle must have to pass.","fact_ids":["sec02-F01","sec02-F02","sec02-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec02-u02","module_id":"sec02-m02","objective_ids":["sec02-u02"],"title":{"text":"Required brakes, lights and gear","fact_ids":["sec02-F03","sec02-F04","sec02-R02"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Brakes, lights and other required gear let you stop, see, and be seen, so inspections check each one.","fact_ids":["sec02-F03","sec02-F04","sec02-F05"]},{"text":"Older cars have a few lighter standards because they were built before modern lighting rules.","fact_ids":["sec02-R02","sec02-R03"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Ken brings his modern car to inspection with one taillight burned out.","fact_ids":["sec02-F04","sec02-R02"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Modern cars need two taillights; only cars built before nineteen sixty may have one.","fact_ids":["sec02-R02","sec02-F04"]},"result":{"text":"Ken replaces the bulb so both taillights work, and the car can pass.","fact_ids":["sec02-R02"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking one working taillight is always enough to pass inspection.","fact_ids":["sec02-R02"]},"correction":{"text":"Only pre-nineteen-sixty cars may have one taillight and one brake light; modern cars need two of each.","fact_ids":["sec02-R02","sec02-F04"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Horn and mirror: two hundred feet.","fact_ids":["sec02-R04","sec02-F05"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A friend's car built last year has one dead brake light. Will it pass?","fact_ids":["sec02-F04","sec02-R02"]},"answer":{"text":"No. Modern cars need two working brake lights.","fact_ids":["sec02-R02"]},"rationale":{"text":"Only pre-nineteen-sixty cars may have one brake light; modern cars need two, plus the center high lamp where one is fitted.","fact_ids":["sec02-R02","sec02-F04"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec02-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"What inspectors look for","fact_ids":["sec02-F03","sec02-F04","sec02-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Brakes, lights, and reflectors.","fact_ids":["sec02-F03","sec02-F04","sec02-F05"]},{"text":"Horn, mirror, tires, and more.","fact_ids":["sec02-F03","sec02-F04","sec02-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers the equipment your vehicle needs to pass inspection. Inspectors check that the vehicle can stop, that it can be seen from every side, and that the driver can see and signal. You will learn the brake standard, the lights and reflectors that are required, how older cars built before nineteen sixty differ, and the other gear such as the horn, mirror, glass, plates, wipers, tires, and fuel cap. Many of these rules come with distances or heights, so pay attention to which number belongs to which piece of equipment as we go.","fact_ids":["sec02-F03","sec02-F04","sec02-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec02-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Brakes that stop and hold","fact_ids":["sec02-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Foot brake: twenty-five feet from twenty.","fact_ids":["sec02-F03"]},{"text":"Parking brake stops and holds.","fact_ids":["sec02-F03"]},{"text":"Both are checked at inspection.","fact_ids":["sec02-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Start with stopping. A safe car needs a foot brake that can stop it within twenty-five feet from a speed of twenty miles per hour. It also needs a parking brake strong enough to stop the car and hold it in place. Those two standards are simple to remember because they describe what each brake is for: the foot brake stops you quickly while moving, and the parking brake keeps the car from rolling once it is stopped. If either brake cannot do its job, the vehicle does not pass inspection, no matter how good the rest of it looks.","fact_ids":["sec02-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec02-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Lights and reflectors","fact_ids":["sec02-F04","sec02-R02","sec02-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Two headlights with a high-beam indicator.","fact_ids":["sec02-F04","sec02-R02","sec02-R03"]},{"text":"Two taillights and two brake lights.","fact_ids":["sec02-F04","sec02-R02","sec02-R03"]},{"text":"Red reflectors, white plate light.","fact_ids":["sec02-F04","sec02-R02","sec02-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Next, lights. A car needs two headlights with a high-beam indicator, two taillights, and two working brake lights, with all three lit where a center high lamp is fitted. Cars built before nineteen sixty may have one taillight and one brake light. The rear plate light must be white. Front parking lights are white or amber, and rear parking lights are red. Two red side reflectors sit fifteen to sixty inches high and must be visible from six hundred feet, or three hundred fifty feet on pre-nineteen-sixty cars. Most vehicles also need electric turn signals.","fact_ids":["sec02-F04","sec02-R02","sec02-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec02-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Horn, mirror, tires, and more","fact_ids":["sec02-F05","sec02-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Horn heard two hundred feet.","fact_ids":["sec02-F05","sec02-R04"]},{"text":"Mirror sees two hundred feet behind.","fact_ids":["sec02-F05","sec02-R04"]},{"text":"Tires hold two thirty-seconds inch.","fact_ids":["sec02-F05","sec02-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"The rest of the required gear covers seeing, signaling, and safety. The horn must be heard from two hundred feet away, and the mirror must show the road two hundred feet behind. Models from nineteen sixty-eight on need emission controls. New and replacement glass must be safety glass. Most vehicles need front and rear plates. You also need wipers, front seat belts where the factory fitted anchorages, tires with at least two thirty-seconds of an inch of tread, and a sound fuel cap on most gasoline vehicles aged two to twenty-four years. Slow vehicles carry a slow-moving emblem.","fact_ids":["sec02-F05","sec02-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec02-u02-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Modern cars versus older cars","fact_ids":["sec02-R02","sec02-R03","sec02-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Modern: two taillights, two brake lights.","fact_ids":["sec02-R02","sec02-R03","sec02-F04"]},{"text":"Before nineteen sixty: one of each.","fact_ids":["sec02-R02","sec02-R03","sec02-F04"]},{"text":"Reflectors: six hundred or three fifty.","fact_ids":["sec02-R02","sec02-R03","sec02-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap built from the older-car exceptions. The handbook gives cars built before nineteen sixty lighter standards, and learners sometimes apply those exceptions to every car. A modern car needs two taillights and two brake lights. Only a pre-nineteen-sixty car may have one of each. The same split applies to reflectors: on a modern car they must be visible from six hundred feet, but on a pre-nineteen-sixty car the standard is three hundred fifty feet. When a question describes a vehicle, check its age first, then pick the matching lighting rule.","fact_ids":["sec02-R02","sec02-R03","sec02-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec02-u02-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the brake lights","fact_ids":["sec02-R02","sec02-F04","sec02-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"A newer car, one dead brake light.","fact_ids":["sec02-R02","sec02-F04","sec02-F05"]},{"text":"Will it pass?","fact_ids":["sec02-R02","sec02-F04","sec02-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: a friend's car was built last year, and one of its two brake lights has burned out. Will it pass inspection? Work out your answer before reading on. No, it will not. Modern cars need two working brake lights, and all three must work where a center high lamp is fitted. The one-light allowance belongs only to cars built before nineteen sixty. Your friend should replace the bulb before the inspection. While at it, it is worth checking that the horn can be heard from two hundred feet away and the tires have enough tread.","fact_ids":["sec02-R02","sec02-F04","sec02-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec02-u02-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Equipment checklist","fact_ids":["sec02-F03","sec02-F04","sec02-R02","sec02-R03","sec02-F05","sec02-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Brakes stop and hold.","fact_ids":["sec02-F03","sec02-F04","sec02-R02","sec02-R03","sec02-F05","sec02-R04"]},{"text":"Required lights and reflectors.","fact_ids":["sec02-F03","sec02-F04","sec02-R02","sec02-R03","sec02-F05","sec02-R04"]},{"text":"Horn and mirror at two hundred feet.","fact_ids":["sec02-F03","sec02-F04","sec02-R02","sec02-R03","sec02-F05","sec02-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"To wrap up, the foot brake must stop the car within twenty-five feet from twenty miles per hour, and the parking brake must stop and hold it. Modern cars need two headlights, two taillights, and two brake lights, while pre-nineteen-sixty cars may have one taillight and one brake light. Reflectors sit fifteen to sixty inches high and show six hundred feet, or three hundred fifty on older cars. The horn is heard and the mirror sees two hundred feet. Add safety glass, plates, wipers, belts, tires with enough tread, and a sound fuel cap. Next, banned and optional gear.","fact_ids":["sec02-F03","sec02-F04","sec02-R02","sec02-R03","sec02-F05","sec02-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec02-u03","module_id":"sec02-m03","objective_ids":["sec02-u03"],"title":{"text":"Banned and optional equipment","fact_ids":["sec02-F06","sec02-R05","sec02-F07"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Some equipment is banned because it could confuse other drivers or interfere with police, like red front lights or radar jammers.","fact_ids":["sec02-F06"]},{"text":"Optional lights are allowed only when they are used in ways that do not blind or mislead other drivers.","fact_ids":["sec02-F07","sec02-R06"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Lee is hauling a ladder that sticks out five inches past the left side of his truck.","fact_ids":["sec02-F06","sec02-R05"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Loads may extend only three inches past the left side, though six inches past the right.","fact_ids":["sec02-R05"]},"result":{"text":"Lee moves the ladder so it does not stick out more than three inches on the left.","fact_ids":["sec02-R05","sec02-F06"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: believing a load may extend the same distance past either side of a vehicle.","fact_ids":["sec02-R05"]},"correction":{"text":"Loads may poke out three inches past the left side but six inches past the right.","fact_ids":["sec02-R05","sec02-F06"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Left three, right six.","fact_ids":["sec02-R05"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A driver approaching oncoming traffic at night has a spotlight on. What should the driver do?","fact_ids":["sec02-F07","sec02-R06"]},"answer":{"text":"Dim or switch off the spotlight for the oncoming drivers.","fact_ids":["sec02-R06"]},"rationale":{"text":"Spotlights must be dimmed for oncoming traffic; they may light the road only when the headlights fail.","fact_ids":["sec02-R06","sec02-F07"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec02-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"What you may not add","fact_ids":["sec02-F06","sec02-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Banned lights and devices.","fact_ids":["sec02-F06","sec02-F07"]},{"text":"Optional lights with rules.","fact_ids":["sec02-F06","sec02-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers equipment from the other direction: what you may not put on a vehicle, and what you may add as long as you follow the rules. Some devices are banned outright because they could confuse other drivers or interfere with police, while others are allowed only when used in certain ways. You will also learn how far a load can stick out past the sides of your vehicle. These rules often come up in practice questions as a description of a vehicle, so the goal is to recognize which items are banned, which are optional, and how each must be used.","fact_ids":["sec02-F06","sec02-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec02-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Banned gear and loads","fact_ids":["sec02-F06","sec02-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"No front red lights or sirens.","fact_ids":["sec02-F06","sec02-R05"]},{"text":"No radar-jamming devices.","fact_ids":["sec02-F06","sec02-R05"]},{"text":"Loads: three left, six right.","fact_ids":["sec02-F06","sec02-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Ordinary vehicles may not carry red lights on the front, bells, sirens, exhaust whistles, muffler cutouts, front flashing red lights, or radar-jamming devices. Emergency vehicles and school or church buses keep their own narrow allowances, but those exceptions do not reach private cars. Loads also have limits. A load may stick out no more than three inches past the left side of a vehicle and no more than six inches past the right side. So the two sides have different limits, and a long load must be packed carefully before you drive, with the left side checked most closely.","fact_ids":["sec02-F06","sec02-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec02-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Optional lights and body height","fact_ids":["sec02-F07","sec02-R06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Body never below the wheel rims.","fact_ids":["sec02-F07","sec02-R06"]},{"text":"Spotlights dim for oncoming traffic.","fact_ids":["sec02-F07","sec02-R06"]},{"text":"Backup lights never burn moving forward.","fact_ids":["sec02-F07","sec02-R06"]}],"narration":{"text":"No car may ride with its body lower than the lowest part of its wheel rims. Optional lights are allowed with rules. Spotlights must be dimmed for oncoming traffic, though they may light fifty feet of road when the headlights fail. Twin cowl lights and single side courtesy lights glow amber or white. Twin backup lights never burn while moving forward. Hazard flashers blink amber or white in front and amber or red in back, all in unison. Up to three extra driving lamps may sit twelve to forty-two inches high, and any window tinting must follow state rules.","fact_ids":["sec02-F07","sec02-R06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec02-u03-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Left three, right six","fact_ids":["sec02-R05","sec02-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Left side limit: three inches.","fact_ids":["sec02-R05","sec02-F06"]},{"text":"Right side limit: six inches.","fact_ids":["sec02-R05","sec02-F06"]},{"text":"Red front lights: emergency only.","fact_ids":["sec02-R05","sec02-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap built from two similar limits. Both sides of a vehicle have a load limit, but they are not the same. A load may extend three inches past the left side and six inches past the right. The tighter limit is on the left, so check that side first. A related trap involves front red lights. They are banned on ordinary vehicles, and only emergency vehicles keep that allowance. So if a question describes a private car with a red light on the front, it is not allowed, no matter how the driver uses it. Measure both sides before every trip with a long load.","fact_ids":["sec02-R05","sec02-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec02-u03-s5","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the spotlight rule","fact_ids":["sec02-R06","sec02-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Oncoming traffic at night.","fact_ids":["sec02-R06","sec02-F07"]},{"text":"Spotlight is on.","fact_ids":["sec02-R06","sec02-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: a driver is heading toward oncoming traffic at night with a spotlight on. What should the driver do with it? Work out your answer before reading on. The driver must dim or switch off the spotlight for the oncoming drivers. A spotlight may light fifty feet of road only when the headlights themselves fail. The same idea of not misleading other drivers explains the backup light rule. Backup lights never burn while moving forward, so other drivers can trust that a car showing backup lights is in reverse.","fact_ids":["sec02-R06","sec02-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec02-u03-s6","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Banned and optional gear","fact_ids":["sec02-F06","sec02-R05","sec02-F07","sec02-R06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Banned: red front lights, sirens, jammers.","fact_ids":["sec02-F06","sec02-R05","sec02-F07","sec02-R06"]},{"text":"Loads: three left, six right.","fact_ids":["sec02-F06","sec02-R05","sec02-F07","sec02-R06"]},{"text":"Optional lights follow strict rules.","fact_ids":["sec02-F06","sec02-R05","sec02-F07","sec02-R06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us sum up. Ordinary vehicles may not carry front red lights, bells, sirens, exhaust whistles, muffler cutouts, front flashing red lights, or radar jammers, while emergency vehicles and school or church buses keep narrow allowances. A load may extend three inches past the left side and six inches past the right. A car's body may not ride below its lowest wheel rims. Spotlights dim for oncoming traffic and light fifty feet only when headlights fail, backup lights never burn moving forward, and hazard flashers blink in unison.
